How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo.

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy, astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere.

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much. At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth. This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed.

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

"Exoplanet" is available now exclusively from Audible. It is free for members of its subscription tiers or available to purchase separately.

One crew. One planet. Three timelines. No one survives alone. A sci-fi thriller executive produced by Andy Weir (#1 bestselling author of Project Hail Mary, The Martian), with an all-star cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo.

Exoplanet is free for Audible members, but also available for purchase separately.

Alix is an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham specialising in the characterisation of stars and exoplanets. She is passionate about science communication, and how astrophysics is portrayed in movies, TV, and pop culture at large.

#821. How Aston Villa are reclaiming their identity

Aston Villa currently sit ninth in the Women's Super League table

A club's true identity always shows in a local derby and Aston Villa hope to impose theirs when they face rivals Birmingham City on Sunday.

Villa have not had a smooth ride of it this season after a winless start led to the sacking of former manager Natalia Arroyo at the end of September.

The Spaniard helped stabilise Villa during her two years in charge but they lacked consistency, and it left some wondering what their identity really was.

Brian Sorensen is the man in charge of changing that on the pitch now, while there are others off it who are transforming Villa behind the scenes.

"Aston Villa is a club of heart. We put a lot into everything we do," managing director Maggie Murphy told BBC Sport.

"I think a lot of people know we try to do everything the right way, the proper way. We're a club that is the heart of 'proper football' in many ways."

So what are Villa doing this season to get in touch with their values?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Former Everton boss Brian Sorensen is now managing Aston Villa

Sunday's Women's Super League match with Birmingham (14:00 GMT) marks 30 years since the team officially took the Aston Villa name.

Sorensen hoes it will be the perfect opportunity to showcase who Villa are on the pitch.

"There's a lot of history in this club which maybe not many people know. We need to showcase that," said interim manager Sorensen.

"We want to be really hard-working and humble - like the area we are from - and have a clear identity of how we attack and defend.

"It's trying to align all of that, making sure that we are a team that is recognised, that is one the other teams will fear playing against."

They will celebrate this crucial point in their history in the second city derby at Villa Park, and inform fans of a research project they are undertaking this season.

The project is called 'Roots, Rise and Reach' and hopes to uncover periods of the women's team's history that have never been documented before.

They have already found a newspaper report from 1957 detailing a game between an unofficial Aston Villa Ladies team and Birmingham City.

"It's huge piece of work that we're doing just to understand our own heritage and where we've come from," said Murphy.

"We're very aware that our roots go much further [than 1996]. We're going back decades at the moment trying to uncover some of that history.

"I think it's really important to know where we've come from, because that gives us a sense of identity that maybe we don't always have."

Diving into the club's history is one way Villa are hoping to engage fans this season.

They are trying to grow attendances as part of the club's five-year strategy and last season set up fan forums for the first time.

In response to feedback, they have changed age categories on their ticketing, introduced hospitality season tickets and hosted podcasts with former players and comedians to improve matchday experiences.

They have also been advertising upcoming games on 'digi-vans' throughout the country in the hope of attracting neutral women's football fans.

"There are plenty of floating fans in women's football so we are trying to grab as many as we can and make sure they have the best possible day," added Murphy.

"They might not support Villa the first time they come, but they might after three, four games and buy themselves a claret and blue scarf.

"That's our drive. We want to build this club sustainably and generate the funds that can then go into the football side of the business."

Villa players are happy stop to sign autographs and take photos after games

All of these efforts are part of a wider club ambition to be sustainable and ultimately deliver success on the pitch.

Murphy's task is to make the women's team financially stable, drive revenue and improve atmosphere at games.

She works in tandem with Marisa Ewers, director of women's football, who oversees recruitment, contract renewals and football staff management.

"We want it to be super coherent across both sides. In a really crude way, my job is to make money and Marissa's job is to spend it," said Murphy.

"Our teams work really closely together. Last year, we only had two people in the club that were 100% dedicated to the women's business side. Today, we have nine.

"We are investing in revenue-generating areas. I definitely want us to be competing at the highest possible level consistently, but with heart.

"We want to feel like we have contributed to the story of women's football in this country."

Villa's season is starting to look up. They currently sit ninth with two wins and four draws from their opening nine matches.

They drew with Arsenal at the start of this month after beating Birmingham City in a penalty shootout in their Women's League Cup tie.

With successive matches against newly promoted sides Birmingham and Charlton coming up, can Villa take a step closer to where they want to be?

"Where we are today is born of the hard work of lots of people that have come before us. We need to recognise that and start to steady the ship," said Murphy.

"Villa has not been in the WSL for that long. People forget that. We're still in a very transitional phase - as is the wider women's football ecosystem."

#820. SKIMS’ New Cryo Globes Look Like Snow Globes and They Sculpt Your Face

Kim Kardashian’s SKIMS collabs on a limited-edition beauty tool that looks like snow globes and it’s made to save winter skin. The glass tools help sculpt and depuff, and make a luxurious gift.

SKIMS continues to innovate, now with a newly launched facial tool with a festive twist. Teaming up with celebrity makeup artist Jenny Patinkin on limited-edition Cryo Glow Globes designed to soothe, sculpt and depuff the face for a glowing complexion.

Beauty holiday gift: Jenny Patinkin x SKIMS Cryo Glow Globes, $78

Patinkin, founder of Eco-Luxe Beauty Tools, called the collaboration a natural fit in an exclusive interview with E!. “Both brands are fundamentally about making women feel more comfortable, confident, and beautiful, without asking them to change who they are,” she said.

The hand-blown glass globes contain floating glitter shaped like snowflakes, candy canes and SKIMS logo sequins, bringing snow-globe energy to your vanity.

Skims' brings its sleek aesthetic to your vanity with these hand-blown glass globes, featuring floating glitter and sequins in festive winter-y motifs.

This marks the first-ever collaboration for the Jenny Patinkin brand, of which has become known for its luxe beauty tools.

“Cryo tools are a quick, easy way to give skin an instantly refreshed, more lifted and more radiant look," said Patinkin, founder of Jenny Patinkin Eco-Luxe Beauty Tools. "The goal is for your skin to look and feel its best, the same way SKIMS makes you look and feel your best.”

Created exclusively for the collaboration, the hand-blown glass globes feature snowflake, candy cane and SKIMS logo sequins floating like in a snow globe. The collaboration brings together Patinkin’s expertise in beauty tools and SKIMS’ signature aesthetic, with the goal of making a sculpting facial ritual easy to incorporate into your everyday routine.

"Cryo Globes are a great way to quickly help get the look of less puffy, more lifted skin," says Patinkin. "The cold temperatures cause a vasoconstriction response in the skin, which can help to create a depuffing effect, and can also help to lock off redness and soothe irritation.

"You can use these tools to give yourself a little lymphatic massage which can aid with the drainage of excess fluids in the skin, and I also find them soothing for sinus pain, headaches, bug bites and sunburns."

Cold, dry weather and a packed holiday calendar can leave skin feeling irritated or puffy. Patinkin says the globes’ cooling effect can help soothe irritation, while gently massaging (similar to a guashua) reduces puffiness for a more sculpted look—an easy at-home facial refresh during the craziest time of year? Now that's a gift worth giving, especially in winter.

"You can use these tools to give yourself a little lymphatic massage which can aid with the drainage of excess fluids in the skin, and I also find them soothing for sinus pain, headaches, bug bites and sunburns."

#819. Declan Rice accepts he had an ‘average World Cup’ as England gear up for Spain showdown

Midfielder needed a break ‘to come back stronger’

James Trafford selected to start in goal for England

Declan Rice has admitted he had an “average” World Cup at the end of a gruelling season and needed time out during the international window in September and October in order to return stronger.

The Arsenal midfielder believes the break has served its purpose, having produced starring performances against Bayern Munich and Liverpool in recent weeks. He is now ready to hit his best level for England in Sunday’s Nations League showdown against Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Rice managed nerve pain in a hamstring that affected his lower back throughout the second half of last season and his fitness was a talking point during the World Cup. The 27-year-old had good games, most notably against the Democratic Republic of the Congo in the last 32 when he filled in towards the end as an emergency right-back.

Rice played well and scored in the third-place playoff against France. But he was typically honest when asked to reflect on his tournament as he prepared for the Spain game. England will leapfrog the world champions and finish top of their Nations League group if – and only if – they win in Madrid. It would theoretically bring an easier draw for the two-leg quarter-finals in March.

“By my standards it was an average World Cup,” Rice said. “France was probably my best game, Congo I played really well; some of the other games I didn’t play too well but you look back … I played 69 games [in the season].

“A title win with Arsenal, a Champions League final loss and into a World Cup. It’s annoying because at the World Cup you want to be at your best, you want to be totally fresh, you want to be ready. It’s annoying that I couldn’t perform how I did at Arsenal towards the back end of the season.

“But knowing if I’m not going to be at my best, just constantly give 100% for this team, for the badge and you could see that. I loved [the last-16 win in] Mexico. We had the disappointment of Argentina in the semi-final, the second group game against Ghana. It’s games you look back on and think: ‘Could I have done better?’”

The playoff against France was on 18 July. After a short break, Rice reported back to Arsenal and played 45 minutes of the Community Shield against Manchester City on 16 August. When he played the 90 minutes of the defeat at Brighton on 19 September, he “did not feel right at all”, leading to a conversation with Tuchel who stood him down from England’s first four Nations League ties, the first of which was the 3-2 loss against Spain at Wembley. Rice sent a voice note to the England captain, Harry Kane, to explain his absence.

“I had an honest conversation with the boss here [Tuchel], who was really understanding,” Rice said. “He said: ‘Take some time, get yourself ready.’ It was about using that time to come back fitter and stronger. I feel really good now. It’s still like I’m building up to being 100 per cent but it’s closer to that than I was a few weeks ago, for sure. And over the last few weeks, my performances have picked up.”

Rice, who won his 81st cap in the win over Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, had only previously withdrawn from three England camps. “I know the importance of playing for England, I know the importance of showing up, being available,” he said. “It’s one of the biggest things to me. Last camp, if I didn’t speak to the manager about it, I wouldn’t have done it. But he gave me his word. So I was in a better place mentally knowing that he authorised it.”

Rice has played at least 50 club matches in each of the past five seasons. “It’s something my body has got used to,” he said. “Probably last year, I felt it more than anything in terms of the amount of games, the toll it does take and realising as you get older, you have to take the recovery side of it a lot more seriously. When you were 21, 22, 23 … you could get up and have a round of golf the next day [after a match]. Now, even though I’m young at 27, you get up after a game and you can hardly feel your legs.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Meanwhile, Tuchel has decided to start James Trafford in goal against Spain – an eye-catching decision that will only harden the impression that Jordan Pickford is no longer his first-choice goalkeeper. Tuchel gave them two matches apiece in the September/ October window and said that he was minded to split the minutes once again this time.

When he started Pickford against Croatia, it felt as though he had shelved the plan, given his insistence that the Everton player remained his No1 and Spain is plainly the bigger game. But Tuchel announced at his pre-match conference that Trafford would be given the opportunity.

“Traff will play,” Tuchel said. “We want to see how far Traff is. So he gets a highly competitive match. We had some changes in the back four in the last match [against Croatia], so we went for more stability and more experience with Pickers. And Traff gets the match tomorrow.

“Hopefully he’s not too over-excited or overly nervous because there’s no need to be. We trust him. But it is different to play for England than to play for your club. And to have the opportunity to play matches where it really matters is the best way to show up and to show that you’re ready. We know what Jordan can do for us. Jordan is, at the moment, our No1. I have a very clear picture in high-pressure moments.”

Tuchel also revealed that Ezri Konsa was back in contention after missing the Croatia game with a minor knee problem. He made it sound as though the Arsenal defender would start. “He showed up yesterday for individual work and he showed up today for training,” Tuchel said. “Ezri is back and ready to play.”

#817. Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain

As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart

Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket. The 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

“He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” says Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

“He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”

Robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at 1 v 1 defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a new era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

Robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here.

“I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show then belief,” he says. “Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin said while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first-team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

“He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”

During a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later, but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and Scott McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October.

“It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” says Robertson. “That’s not really me.”

Modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program and set the stage for the Apollo progam to land on the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin. NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program. Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11, and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13.

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview. "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station. As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon.

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

#814. Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’

The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places

“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal: When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation.

Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams

I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I said to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an issue because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.

I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan

I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.

Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia

My feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.

Maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David

If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?

In the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze

We did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a big squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.

What was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish

His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone says that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through, so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.

What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre

Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.

Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous

I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.

I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim

We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.

I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

#813. Taylor Frankie Paul's Ex Dakota Mortensen Suing Hulu for Defamation

Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Dakota Mortensen, who has appeared on the Hulu reality show alongside his ex Taylor Frankie Paul, has filed a lawsuit against the network, alleging staged events.

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives alum—who has appeared on the Hulu reality series with his now-ex Taylor Frankie Paul—has filed a lawsuit against the network, as well as Jeff Jenkins Productions and Ludwig Productions, according to court documents obtained by multiple outlets Nov. 13.

In his suit, the 33-year-old alleged that seasons three, four, and five of the series presented him "to millions of viewers as a domestic abuser," per court documents obtained by local outlet ABC4 Utah, "as a man who retaliated against the mother of his child by reporting her to Child Protective Services, and as a serial adulterer.”

Earlier this year, a legal battle between Mortensen and Paul—who share a 2-year-old son—began after he filed to request a protective order against on her on the same day that TMZ published a video of a 2023 physical altercation featuring the former couple.

In April, Paul—who is also mom to two kids with ex-husband Tate Paul—then requested her own temporary restraining order, alleging Mortensen had a "pattern of abusive conduct and coercive control" throughout their on-again, off-again romance.

Later that month, per Today, a judge granted mutual protective orders.

Mortensen also alleges in his lawsuit against the network that producers created storylines "assembled from staged events and from the deliberate deletion of footage that contradicted the storyline, and published after the producers had been informed by Mortensen and by others, that the allegations were false."

More specifically, Mortensen alleges cameras captured Paul striking Mortensen with a pizza box while filming season five, per ABC 4 Utah, and demanded that the footage be included in the episodes that aired, but that it was excluded from the final cut.

E! News has reached out to Paul’s reps for comment about the alleged incident.

“The knowingly false portrayal of Mortensen as the abuser in the relationship continued uninterrupted," the suit states, "while the only footage of physical aggression between the two, aggression by Paul against Mortensen, was intentionally withheld from viewers to promote a false narrative."

Mortensen is asking for compensatory damages, ABC 4 Utah reports, as well as other damages. E! News has reached out to Hulu and Mortensen's attorney for comment and has not yet heard back.

In mid-April, Paul was granted supervised visitation with her and Mortensen's son and one week later, the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office announced in a news release it would not be filing charges against her after completing two separate investigations led by the Draper Police Department and West Jordan Police Department.

For his part, Mortensen previously described the situation between the two as “deeply upsetting.”

“I am focusing on our son and his safety,” he told E! News in a statement in March, “and hope that Taylor will do the same.”

For a closer look at the timeline of the allegations made between Paul and Mortensen, keep reading…

Feb. 17, 2023: Taylor Frankie Paul Arrested Following Confrontation With Dakota Mortensen

After rising to fame with #MomTok, Taylor Frankie Paul was arrested in Utah on Feb. 17, 2023 stemming from an incident with then boyfriend Dakota Mortensen. She was accused of throwing metal chairs and a wooden playset at him while one of her two children—who she shares with ex-husband Tate Paul—was in the room, per an affidavit obtained by ABC 4 Utah.

Paul was charged with one count of felony aggravated assault, two counts of felony domestic violence in the presence of a child causing injury, one count of misdemeanor child abuse and one count of misdemeanor criminal mischief, according to court documents released by the District Attorney for Salt Lake County and obtained by E! News at the time.

A Herriman Police Department officer who responded to the incident said that when he arrived, Mortensen "reported he was in an argument with his girlfriend,” according to a written declaration in the court documents. The officer further stated that "during the argument, Mortensen attempted to leave the residence, however [Paul] began hitting him."

August 2023: Taylor Frankie Paul Pleads Guilty to Aggravated Assault

Paul pleaded guilty to a third-degree felony count of aggravated assault in August 2023, according to court documents obtained by the Salt Lake Tribune, while four other charges were dismissed with prejudice.

Her plea was held in abeyance for three years, at which time the charge would be entered as a Class A misdemeanor as long as Paul abided by the terms of her plea agreement, per the documents.

According to her plea deal, Paul was to obtain both a substance abuse evaluation and a domestic violence evaluation and complete any recommended treatment over a three-year period—as well as not violate any major laws.

March 19, 2024: Taylor Frankie Paul and Dakota Mortensen Welcome Son

Paul and Mortensen's son was born a week early, with Paul posting a photo from the hospital to Instagram on April 4, 2024 and writing, “We’ve had the best two weeks with him. We all love you so much, thank you for blending our family.”

September 2024: Taylor Frankie Paul Speaks Out About 2023 Arrest

Paul admitted in an interview with E! News that the altercation with Mortensen was their “rock bottom for sure.”

"He stood by me with that because he knew everything going on behind closed doors,” she said. “That was a horrible night and I'm full of regret. Dakota has been at rock bottom himself, so he could totally relate. He was like, 'I want to help you out of this.'"

As for the confrontation itself, she later said the incident had been building up.

“I had an ectopic [pregnancy] a few months prior, and then I had a chemical pregnancy,” she shared on the Viall Files podcast in September 2024. “I don't want to blame hormones, but I will put that into account. Like, I am pretty whack.”

Paul added that the events had left her feeling lost and angry, saying, "I was feeling so low I went and drank that night. And Dakota picks me up and he’s angry that I drank."

"I remember throwing things, and I don't know my daughters on the couch. We had babysitters there, so I think they’re upstairs sleeping," she said, alleging that Mortensen tried to tell her that her then 5-year-old daughter was present, but "I'm like so gone I don’t care, and I throw another chair."

Sept. 6, 2024: Secret Lives of Mormon Wives Premieres

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives debuted on Hulu in September 2024, with the first episode of season one featuring Paul's 2023 arrest.

May 18, 2025: Taylor Frankie Paul Confirms Dakota Mortensen Breakup After On-Again, Off-Again Relationship

Paul confirmed their split in May 2025 after it was revealed on the season two premiere of SLOMW that Mortensen had cheated on her shortly after they had welcomed their son, writing on TikTok, "Dakota isn’t mine anymore, wish him the best.”

"Dakota and I were living together and in bliss with our new baby, and I was even considering engagement,” she said on the premiere episode. “And then I learned that he was lying this entire time.”

During a season four episode of SLOMW, Mortensen admitted to cheating with their friend Shinia Powell, telling Taylor during a FaceTime call, “Was it dumb of me? Yes. Could I have picked someone else? Yes. Who it was matters, and that's where I think I went wrong. I picked somebody that was obviously going to come with problems, and that was very s--tty of me to do."

Sept. 10, 2025: Taylor Frankie Paul Is Cast as The Bachelorette for Season 22

In a surprising turn of events, Paul was cast as the leading lady for season 22 of The Bachelorette, confirming the news during an appearance on Call Her Daddy in September 2025. The decision marked a notable departure for the franchise, as it usually casts suitors from previous seasons of The Bachelor in the position.

But for Paul, it was a welcome change, saying in a teaser for the season, “I do believe I was gifted this for another chapter in my life.”

“I’ve been criticized, I’ve been judged and I’ve been rejected,” Paul continued, “but anyone that takes the time to know me will see that I’m actually a genuine person and I mean well and a person that deserves another chance at love.”

#812. Respect? Exposure? Why England's star names are going abroad

Anthony Gordon joined Barcelona from Newcastle in the summer

Bayern Munich's Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane, Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham, Barcelona's Anthony Gordon - three of England's star players, all of whom are playing their club football abroad.

The Premier League is widely regarded as the most competitive league in the world with the greatest financial muscle, but that does not always translate to the biggest individual profiles and, increasingly, star names are looking elsewhere.

Since Cristiano Ronaldo won the Ballon d'Or in 2008, for example, only Rodri in 2024 was playing in England at the time of being crowned the best player in the world. Michael Owen, in 2001, was the last Englishman to do so while in England.

The trend of English players going abroad has gathered pace since a teenage Jadon Sancho signed for Borussia Dortmund in 2017 and that is reflected in this current Three Lions squad - seven of the initial 25 play outside England.

"Jude Bellingham and Harry Kane were decisive for us in the World Cup and I see no reason they won't be in the future," said England boss Thomas Tuchel when talking about his big stars playing outside of their home country.

"It's good that Anthony has stepped up now. He is the third one. There is obviously a relevance to them playing abroad but I don't see that a player who plays in the Premier League cannot step up and be decisive for us."

At the World Cup in the summer and during the last international break, however, it was those three players' goals and assists that proved decisive.

Currently there are 43 English players on the Football Association's radar playing their club football in Europe.

The FA's technical director John McDermott believes it is a "huge positive" to have so many players playing across Europe.

"I spoke to a couple of the boys that are playing abroad at the moment," he told BBC Sport. "The exposure they get in those leagues, playing Champions League or European football, where you're not necessarily having to bang out 55 games, but you still have got time to do your weight training and your gym work.

"Often if you're playing in the English competition or in the EFL, where it's 46 games - you know it's game, game, game, which is fantastic - but for some players that opportunity to get the training in-between and to practise developing on technique or other areas, there's benefits to that."

McDermott was previously at Tottenham Hotspur and says that even when he was in club football, he was a "big believer" in players going abroad to "develop character" and "independence".

"I think being in another changing room and learning another language just puts you under the pressure to adapt," he added.

"And I think for any young person that ability not only to become technically, tactically more adept, but also culturally have to pick up something else - it's huge and prevents people from becoming complacent or just getting used to the same old, same old."

Gordon said in the recent international break he feels he gets more respect now he plays for one of Europe's elite sides, compared with when he was at Newcastle.

"I think he's always been respected," McDermott said.

"I remember when Trips (Kieran Trippier) came back, and Trips was a good player, but when he came back from Atletico (Madrid) I noticed he was just maybe tighter technically and noticed there was a change that Kieran came back with.

"So I'm not sure if he's respected more ... but I think you want all of the players - whether they stay in England [or not] - every six months you see this sort of incremental step where they've added something, another dimension to the game.

"That can sometimes come in this country, obviously, playing with different players, being in new competitions, but I think going abroad definitely helps that.

"And I've seen that with Anthony already and some of the other boys. They come back, it's four months since you've seen them and there's another dimension there."

McDermott is keen to make clear that developing in England can still be of a huge benefit and that Jarell Quansah and Jobe Bellingham, two of England's squad who are now playing in Germany, also played in the EFL.

"There's all different ways, I don't think there's this elixir, I don't think there's this magic formula, 'this is the way'," McDermott said.

England reached the semi-finals of the World Cup for just the third time in their history in the summer.

McDermott was asked if he thought now the Three Lions had more players abroad, it could help develop England's style or performance in major tournaments.

"Yeah, possibly. Again don't underestimate if you're playing now in the Champions League at an English club," he said.

"We would like more players in the pipeline. I think at the moment we're on about 26% or 27% English-qualified players playing the Premier League.

"We've got 40 to 50 players playing at Champions League quality and playing in European football, top Premier League clubs, so let's not underestimate our own product."

McDermott says it is clear the impact having players in different countries is having on the squad, but it is then down to the manager to blend the style.

"I think the different cultural experiences they get, the different exposure they get to play in different types of football is fantastic.

"But still, the England manager has got to try and find that singular blend when they come back of the English players, the Spanish players, the German players, the Italian players, it's all sort of an eclectic mix that they're bringing."

England's record goalscorer, appearance maker and captain Harry Kane is playing his club football in Germany with Bayern Munich, while Jude Bellingham has never played in the Premier League - leaving Birmingham for Borussia Dortmund and now Real Madrid

Gordon has impressed since making his move to Barcelona in the summer with three goals and five assists in 15 appearances in all competitions.

The 25-year-old is regularly lining up with some of the best players in the world, in a front line alongside Lamine Yamal and Raphinha.

The lure of European giants like Real Madrid, Barcelona and Bayern Munich is hard for any player to turn down.

Arsenal's approach for Vinicius Jr this summer was always going to be hard to complete as the famous white shirt and lifestyle in Madrid is, for most players, the pinnacle.

But does moving abroad to one of Europe's top clubs also alter people's perceptions of English players?

"I always felt in England, people respected me because I was fast and I pressed, but they never actually respected the quality and IQ that I play with," Gordon said in a recent interview with ITV.

"Only the players I play with ever seem to notice that. I think now I'm at Barcelona and I play a different style, those qualities are highlighted much more and people are actually starting to take notice that I'm not just quick."

Gordon produced some standout moments in the World Cup, assisting both of Kane's goals in the last-32 win over DR Congo, winning a penalty in England's last-16 win over Mexico and scoring the goal to put England ahead in the semi-final against Argentina.

Captain Kane said the winger is "showing that he belongs at the highest level, for Barcelona and England" and that Gordon is "relishing" being one of England's "main men".

"I think it's great," added England and Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin. "The fact that we've got top-level English players playing abroad now at top European clubs, I think it's only good for English football and us as a national team.

"You see they bring different experiences that they're learning from overseas and they bring it into this group and I think as you can see they're only growing in confidence and as players and I think it's only a positive thing."

Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.

As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now."Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.

The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website, the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old. The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.

This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA.

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.

"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement.

"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

#810. Sam Hartman's Agent Reveals If Bachelor Will Affect Football Schedule

After Washington Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman was announced as the lead of The Bachelor season 30, his agent shared whether the ABC series would affect his time on the field.

Sam Hartman's season on The Bachelor may be quite the blitz.

After the Washington Commanders quarterback was selected as the top pick for season 30, one of his agents shared whether his search for love on the ABC series will impact his time on the field.

In fact, though the series is expected to premiere in March, the NFL star—who joined the Commanders as an undrafted free agent in 2024—shouldn't be on the end of any interceptions.

"[Filming schedule is still being worked out to accommodate the [Commanders] schedule,” Hartman's agent Brian McLaughlin told ESPN’s Kalyn Kahler Nov. 13. “He did run it by the team and they understood."

And when it came to the aspect of handing over his cell phone once filming started, McLaughlin joked that he might find a way to steal Hartman for a sec. (The show's production will overlap with the NFL free agency come March 11.)

"I plan on standing outside the mansion and yelling offers to him over the gate," he told Kahler. "I'll call the mansion landline, worst case scenario."

The glimpse into Hartman's potential shake-up comes after the 27-year-old shared his disbelief about becoming the next Bachelor lead.

"I’m excited but also very nervous," Hartman admitted on Good Morning America Nov. 13. "I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl. 30 is going to be pretty tough."

However, as Hartman joked, he likely won't need to huddle up with his squad for any words of wisdom.

“My teammates were giving me some advice on the plane ride back,” the NFL player said. “So probably not going to listen to anybody on that. But no, I'm excited.”

As for who else is thrilled, Hartman's loved ones are ready for his journey to begin as well.

“They're excited,” he said of his family. “My mom and I have a really cool relationship, and my pops is obviously just supportive. And their big thing is just be myself and enjoy the experience, and you know, trust the instincts and trust your gut.”

Until Hartman makes his rosy debut, take a look at where other Bachelor Nation couples stand today...

Lest the couple forget where their journey began, they need only walk past the master bedroom in their Dallas-area pad. That's where the graphic designer has framed the final final rose that season 17's Bachelor presented her back in that Thai forest in late 2012, right after he promised to tell her he loved her every day of the rest of their lives.

"It made sense to dry this one and make it permanent because it was accompanied by a ring and a proposal, so this is a really special thing," Catherine explained to Entertainment Tonight in 2017. Because that last rose ceremony, complete with an elephant ride and a $75,000 Neil Lane diamond, is as much part of their story as the the sweet, suburban life that followed with kids Samuel, 5, Isaiah, 3, and Mia, 2. "We don't want to shy away from the fact that we got engaged and fell in love on The Bachelor," she said, "so that is the only red rose I will allow in my house!"

The OG Bachelorette, Trista was the first to prove that a stint in the mansion could lead to love, marriage and even Bachelor babies. "Nowadays they shoot the show for, I believe, three months. So it's like 12 weeks," the author shared with Us Weekly of her 2003 season. "My show was shot in six weeks. So Ryan and I met, got engaged, got married a year later, after knowing each other for six weeks. So that's how it used to be."Their decade years holding it down as the show's success story have taught the Colorado-based pair they can handle pretty much anything. Including months sheltering in place with their kids, son Maxwell, 14, and daughter Blakesley, 13. "It's really hard for us to get a date night. I think when the kids are working, we try to take advantage of that time as much as possible," she said of scheduling around the firefighter's early bird tendencies. "But yeah, we're good. We're 16 years and this too shall pass, as they say."

Who even remembers that the sweet divorced dad originally proposed to Melissa Rycroft? Okay, probably a lot of people, as his 2009 After the Final Rose switcheroo still ranks as one of the series' most shocking moments. But if all's well that end's well, the only thing that matters is that the Seattle-based parents to daughter Riley marked 10 years of marriage this past February. "Let me apologize publicly again for putting you through the Bachelor mess that I created," Jason, also dad to teen Ty, wrote in an anniversary tribute. "With that being said... it built an incredible, unique, foundation for us to build our family—showing that we can make it through anything."

In true Bachelor fashion, native Tennesseean Peyton simply knew when she laid eyes on her future husband. Though it wasn't season 10 lead Andy Baldwin. Nearly four years after the naval officer sent her home, the Bachelor Pad alum turned up at another series-related event in 2010 and spied Chris, fresh off his showing as Ali Fedotowsky's runner-up. "It's one of those things where I've had a ton of serious relationships," she later explained to People, "and I met this kid and he was genuine, outgoing and hilarious and we just click."By the following June, the landscaper was proposing at his home in Cape Cod. And more than a decade, two kids (daughter Lyla, 5, and son Hayes, 3) and a few HGTV and DIY Network shows later, they credit the series with laying their foundation. As Peyton put it in an August 2020 Instagram post, "Without the show I'm not sure our paths would have ever crossed."

For as much as the wedding dress designer seemed to key in on Brooks Forester during her 2013 season, it was sweet mortgage lender Chris and his thoughtful prose that proved to be the perfect fit. More than seven years after their L.A. vows (during which the Desiree Hartsock Bridal designer wore two of her own original creations) they're settled in Portland, Oregon, with sons Asher, 5, and Zander, 3. "If our life were a storybook I would be the damsel in distress," the host of podcast Heart of Purpose surmised in a February 2020 post. "Chris would be the funny yet charming knight who saves the day, Asher would be the pragmatic problem solver while his little brother would be the carefree sidekick trying to kiss all the ladies!" And they would all enjoy a happy ending. As Desiree put it in a post acknowledging the choice of Clare Crawley as Bachelorette, "Reality TV worked for me!"

The gold standard in Paradise success stories, the married duo have inspired countless rose seekers to turn up in Mexico with visions of Neil Lane diamonds and Chris Harrison-officiated vows dancing in their heads. The couple's time on the spin-off's second season yielded both, and with son Reed's November 2020 arrival, they'll tie the Lowes for most Bachelor offspring. "Life gets crazy sometimes," Jade wrote in a January anniversary post of juggling 4-year-old daughter Emmy and 2-year-old son Brooks, "but I wouldn't want to go through this hand-in-hand with anyone but you. I would choose you 1000 times over."

When the Bachelor in Paradise alum returned to the beaches of Nayarit, he was initially hesitant to pursue the Bachelor finalist, worried his peripatetic lifestyle wouldn't "mesh" with the former beauty queen's. But nearly three years (plus one brief breakup and a scary December 2019 ski accident that saw Dean laid up in Switzerland for weeks) later, they, and the van he calls home, are jelling just fine. "Obviously I was wrong about that because things are going well," he shared on his podcast Help! I Suck at Dating in October 2019, months before they started wearing rings to show their shared commitment. Mostly, he appreciates that she has a healthy level of snark and the ability to handle his jokes. "I can be myself around her," he continued. "Which is a nice change."

Though he skipped the Neil Lane-sponsored proposal on Bachelor in Paradise in 2018, Kevin was ready to take a knee by the following fall, proposing in his native Toronto where he and Astrid share a home. While they've since had to push off their planned November 2020 vows in her Florida hometown, "We're actually okay with it," Astrid wrote on Instagram, noting that making the decision to postpone due to the coronavirus pandemic allowed them to focus on their connection more than the myriad wedding details. "I wouldn't want to tackle 2020 & the rest of life with anyone else by my side." Now "back in the full swing of wedding planning," as she put it on Instagram, they'll wed this October just weeks before son August's first birthday.

Even the most wishful of Bachelorette fans likely weren't betting on JoJo and Jordan's journey leading them to an altar. Because with the persistent rumors of the former Vanderbilt quarterback's ill intentions ramping up even before they took the stage for the requisite grin-and-gush After the Final Rose appearance in 2016, it seemed unlikely she would still be wearing her 3.75-carat Neil Lane diamond years later.Which, she's not. But only because Jordan presented the real estate developer with an upgrade in August 2019. Though their summer 2020 wedding plans were scrapped due to the pandemic ("I know it will be all more worth the wait," JoJo wrote in a post acknowledging their would-be June day), they tied the knot in May 2022. "You make me laugh, love me endlessly, encourage me to be brave, and always, without fail, are my biggest cheerleader," the native Texan wrote in a post on their fourth anniversary. "Can't wait for what the rest of our lives have in store for us."

Consider Ashley the poster child for ignoring all of the standard he's-just-not-that-into-you signs. Because after four years of lusting for the guy she declared her dream man upon sight, she was proven right at their August 2019 vows in Newport, R.I. Every bit as all-in as his bride, who welcomed their son Dawson in January, Jared reflected on their perfect day on Instagram, writing, "Ashley is my best friend, my person, my soulmate and now my wife. I love this woman more than words will ever allow me to express."

Who needs Neil Lane and a beach backdrop when you have this much imagination? The Dallas-based real estate agent went big when proposing to his Paradise love in May 2019. "She thought it was a normal shoot day," Adam told E! News of his plan to turn a set-up for her online boutique into an impromptu engagement session. "We were at the helicopter pad on the roof and Raven had roses in her hand. She was throwing the petals up for cute photos. She did a few practice runs and then the videographer slipped me the ring and once she threw the petals up, I got down on one knee. I blacked out, but I got everything out that I wanted."

Three months after their April 2021 vows, she announced she was expecting son Gates. "OVER THE MOON EXCITED TO SHARE THE NEWS!" she wrote on social media. "I've loved you before you were in my womb!" Raven and Adam welcomed the child in January 2022.

Sure, she waffled a bit in the early days of Paradise, unsure if her heart belonged to Barbour or Blake Horstmann, but once she zeroed in on the tech entrepreneur, she truly committed. Now the California-based duo are busying themselves with putting together their dream nuptials. While Barbour is set on a good DJ and "maybe an In-N-Out truck," Godwin is thinking big picture. "I have a few little things saved on social media," she told E! News in November 2019. "I have such fun ideas, but good weather, a cool view and a really good time. That's the one thing we do talk about and reiterate."

So he pulled a Mesnick? More than three years after Bachelor Arie dumped onetime fiancée Becca Kufrin on-air to start things up again with Lauren, the pair are married (Chris Harrison officiated their January 2019 wedding in Hawaii, natch), loving life with their 2-year-old daughter Alessi and 11-month-old twins Lux and Senna and perfecting the art of getting through tough times together. Following a heartbreaking 2020 miscarriage, Arie gifted his bride with an eternity band symbolizing "that we will always have each other in our darkest times," Lauren explained. "i think it's safe to say he gets husband of the year." To hear Arie tell it, though, makes him the lucky one. "The fact is, I'm really happy with Lauren," he told GQ in 2018 of their origin story. "So for me, it was all worth it."

#809. Wenger decides not to challenge Fifa chief Infantino

Arsene Wenger had considered running for the Fifa presidency

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger has decided not to stand against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in Fifa's presidential election.

The Frenchman had been considering running for the job but sources have told BBC Sport that he has ruled himself out.

Current world football chief Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Wenger - who is Fifa's head of global development - would have had the backing of European football's governing body Uefa, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino.

On Saturday, French newspaper L'Equipe reported that Wenger was unlikely, external to challenge his boss.

Wenger has credibility throughout the footballing world, and this will be a significant boost to Infantino as he seeks a fourth term as president.

Uefa is said to still be hopeful of finding an alternative candidate before Wednesday's deadline.

One influential figure in the group of stakeholders opposed to Infantino told BBC Sport the news was "a real shame".

"Even if not perfect, I do think he could have galvanized many around the world," they added.

Infantino laughs off resignation questions

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

However, sources have told BBC Sport that the 68-year-old has not yet secured the necessary five endorsements from member associations ahead of Wednesday's deadline but is "still fighting hard".

Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Infantino has retained support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.
